claim: Ubx protein is not distributed uniformly in nuclei but exhibits regions of high and low Ubx intensities.
source: We found that Ubx protein was not distributed uniformly, but rather exhibited regions of high and low Ubx intensities (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining and confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: Nuclei of expanded embryos contain on average 185 ± 25 clusters per nucleus that are stronger than one-quarter of the maximum Ubx intensity.
source: We observed, on average, 185 ± 25 (n = 12, three embryos) clusters per nucleus that were stronger than one-quarter of the maximum Ubx intensity within that nucleus (Figure 1D,E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from expansion microscopy data across 12 nuclei from three embryos

claim: Engrailed (En) displays non-uniform sub-nuclear concentrations that only partially overlap with Ubx distribution.
source: Engrailed (En), a transcription factor unrelated to Ubx, displayed non-uniform sub-nuclear concentrations, but its distribution only partially overlapped with that of Ubx (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C, white regions indicate overlap).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence staining data showing spatial distributions of En and Ubx

claim: Even-skipped (Eve) only partially overlaps with Ubx distribution.
source: We similarly observed only partial overlap between Ubx and Even-skipped (Eve) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence staining data showing spatial distributions of Eve and Ubx

claim: Abdominal-A (AbdA) is excluded from Ubx regions in nuclei where both are expressed.
source: Abdominal-A (AdbA), a paralog of Ubx that is expressed mainly in separate cells from Ubx and that has similar DNA-binding specificity as Ubx, was excluded from Ubx regions in the few nuclei where both were expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence staining data showing spatial distributions of AbdA and Ubx

claim: The distributions of transcription factors En, Eve, and AbdA do not result from a shared mechanism that limits distribution to the same sub-nuclear regions.
source: These results indicate that the distributions of these transcription factors do not result from a shared mechanism that limits the distribution of all transcription factors to the same sub-nuclear regions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different transcription factors show distinct, non-overlapping distribution patterns

claim: Active RNA Polymerase II (Pol II, Ser5 phosphorylated CTD) only partially overlaps with Ubx distribution.
source: Both active RNA Polymerase II (Pol II, Ser5 phosphorylated CTD) and the methylated histone H3K4me3, which marks actively transcribed DNA, only partially overlapped with Ubx (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence staining data showing spatial distributions of active Pol II and Ubx

claim: The methylated histone H3K4me3 only partially overlaps with Ubx distribution.
source: Both active RNA Polymerase II (Pol II, Ser5 phosphorylated CTD) and the methylated histone H3K4me3, which marks actively transcribed DNA, only partially overlapped with Ubx (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence staining data showing spatial distributions of H3K4me3 and Ubx

claim: The histone mark H3K27me3 displays almost no overlap with the distribution of Ubx.
source: In contrast, the histone mark H3K27me3, which marks regions of repressed chromatin, displayed almost no overlap with the distribution of Ubx (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G–I).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence staining data showing spatial distributions of H3K27me3 and Ubx

claim: Ubx is not merely restricted to regions inside the nucleus that are available to transcription factors or to regions of high transcriptional activity.
source: Thus, Ubx is not merely restricted to regions inside the nucleus that are available to transcription factors or to regions of high transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the partial overlap patterns with active transcription markers and lack of overlap with repressed chromatin markers

claim: HaloTag-Ubx protein retains expected Ubx behavior as demonstrated by transformation of anterior segments to posterior segment fate.
source: Over-expression of the HaloTag-Ubx transgene by incubating the embryos at 30°C transformed anterior segments to the fate of more posterior segments, indicated by the presence of additional trichomes. This result indicates that the HaloTag-Ubx protein retains the expected Ubx behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: Functional assay showing phenotypic transformation in cuticle preparations

claim: Individual HaloTag-Ubx molecules bind to specific nuclear domains with residence times on the order of a second before dissociation.
source: We found that fluorescence signals over time changed in discrete up or down steps, indicating that individual HaloTag-Ubx molecules bind to specific nuclear domains with residence times on the order of a second before dissociation.
evidence: Live imaging data showing stepwise changes in fluorescence intensity over time

claim: Most unbound Ubx molecules move too quickly to be captured with 100 ms exposure time.
source: Most unbound Ubx molecules move too quickly to be captured with the 100 ms exposure time; they move in and out of a diffraction-limited region in significantly less than 100 ms on average.
evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of molecule dynamics

claim: The timescales of Ubx binding dynamics are consistent with transcription factor-DNA binding dynamics measured in mammalian cell lines.
source: These timescales are consistent with transcription factor-DNA binding dynamics measured in live-cell imaging experiments using mammalian cell lines (Liu et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2011; Normanno et al., 2015; Morisaki et al., 2014; Gebhardt et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison with published studies on transcription factor dynamics in mammalian cells

claim: Repeated binding events of Ubx produce high intensities in time-averaged projections and indicate that Ubx concentrates and remains within specific nuclear regions.
source: These repeated binding events produced the high intensities observed in the time-averaged projections and indicate that Ubx concentrates and remains within specific nuclear regions.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of time-averaged fluorescence data

claim: Binding of Ubx to DNA is required to generate restricted nuclear distributions of Ubx.
source: These results suggest that binding of Ubx to DNA is required to generate restricted nuclear distributions of Ubx.
evidence: Comparison of wild-type Ubx with DNA-binding deficient mutant (R3A N51A) showing loss of spatial heterogeneity in the mutant

claim: The mutant HaloTag-Ubx (R3A N51A) does not display spatial heterogeneity and exhibits only extremely brief fluctuations in intensity inconsistent with transcription-factor DNA-binding events.
source: The mutant HaloTag-Ubx (R3A N51A) did not display spatial heterogeneity and exhibited only extremely brief fluctuations in intensity inconsistent with transcription-factor DNA-binding events (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: Live imaging data of DNA-binding deficient Ubx mutant

claim: Active svb transcription sites colocalize with areas of high Ubx concentration spanning approximately a few hundred nanometers.
source: Thus, active svb transcription sites colocalized with areas of high Ubx concentration spanning approximately a few hundred nanometers.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of radially averaged Ubx intensity around svb transcription sites

claim: The normalized Ubx intensity at the site of svb transcription was 0.60 ± 0.17 and decreased approximately 250 nm away from the site.
source: The normalized Ubx intensity after background subtraction at the site of svb transcription was 0.60 ± 0.17 (n = 59, four embryos, uncertainty is the variance of the background) and decreased approximately 250 nm away from the site.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis of Ubx around svb transcription sites

claim: Transcription at a locus not regulated by Ubx does not show Ubx enrichment on average.
source: Indeed, we observed that active transcription sites driven by a synthetic enhancer containing binding sites for a TALEA transcription factor (Crocker et al., 2016a; Crocker and Stern, 2013; Crocker et al., 2017) did not show Ubx enrichment on average despite wide fluctuations in Ubx levels, with a relative enrichment of Ubx at TALEA-driven enhancers of 0.02 ± 0.63 (Figure 3A–C, n = 29, three embryos).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of Ubx distribution around transcription sites driven by synthetic TALEA enhancer

claim: The svb locus on homologous X chromosomes often co-localizes to the same Ubx microenvironment.
source: In numerous nuclei actively transcribing svb on the X chromosome, we observed what appeared to be two transcription sites within 200 nm of each other (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B). This indicates that the svb locus on homologous X chromosomes often co-localizes to the same Ubx microenvironment.
evidence: Spatial analysis of svb transcription sites in nuclei showing close proximity of homologous loci

claim: The native svb locus and ectopic svb enhancers co-localize often in nuclei in which both are transcribed.
source: Double-FISH experiments revealed that the native svb locus and the ectopic svb enhancer co-localized often in nuclei in which both were transcribed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Double-FISH experimental data showing spatial colocalization

claim: The transcription sites of forkhead (fkh) do not colocalize with the svb locus.
source: In contrast, the transcription sites of forkhead (fkh, also on chromosome 3) did not colocalize with the svb locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Double-FISH experimental data showing spatial separation

claim: The average distance between pairs of related transcription sites (svb-svb, svb-7H, and svb-E3N) within single nuclei is approximately 250 nm.
source: The average distance between pairs of related transcription sites (svb-svb, svb-7H, and svb-E3N) within single nuclei is approximately 250 nm, near the resolution limit of AiryScan images (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Quantitative distance measurements from double-FISH experiments

claim: fkh and svb transcription sites are on average 1 µm apart.
source: On the other hand, fkh and svb transcription sites are on average 1 µm apart.
evidence: Quantitative distance measurements from double-FISH experiments

claim: Related enhancers co-localize in transcriptional microenvironments independently of their chromosomal location.
source: These results indicate that related enhancers co-localize in transcriptional microenvironments independently of their chromosomal location.
evidence: Inferred from observation that svb enhancers on different chromosomes colocalize while unrelated enhancers do not

claim: Transcription factor microenvironments are highly differentiated and related enhancers often exploit the same transcriptional microenvironments.
source: This suggests that transcription factor microenvironments are highly differentiated and that related enhancers often exploit the same transcriptional microenvironments.
evidence: Inferred from colocalization patterns of related vs. unrelated enhancers

claim: Transcription sites driven by relocated svb enhancers DG3, E3N, and 7hr colocalize with regions of high Ubx concentration.
source: Transcription sites driven by these relocated enhancers also colocalized with regions of high Ubx concentration (Figure 3D).
evidence: FISH and immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of enhancer-driven transcription with Ubx

claim: The relative Ubx enrichment for DG3 enhancer is 0.56 ± 0.16.
source: The relative Ubx enrichment for each of the three enhancers was 0.56 ± 0.16 for DG3 (n = 61, three embryos), 0.51 ± 0.19 for E3N (n = 142, 11 embryos), and 0.68 ± 0.10 for 7 hr (n = 38, three embryos) (Figure 3E–H,M,N).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis

claim: The relative Ubx enrichment for E3N enhancer is 0.51 ± 0.19.
source: The relative Ubx enrichment for each of the three enhancers was 0.56 ± 0.16 for DG3 (n = 61, three embryos), 0.51 ± 0.19 for E3N (n = 142, 11 embryos), and 0.68 ± 0.10 for 7 hr (n = 38, three embryos) (Figure 3E–H,M,N).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis

claim: The relative Ubx enrichment for 7hr enhancer is 0.68 ± 0.10.
source: The relative Ubx enrichment for each of the three enhancers was 0.56 ± 0.16 for DG3 (n = 61, three embryos), 0.51 ± 0.19 for E3N (n = 142, 11 embryos), and 0.68 ± 0.10 for 7 hr (n = 38, three embryos) (Figure 3E–H,M,N).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis

claim: Low-affinity enhancers actively transcribed far from the native svb locus also co-localize with microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations.
source: These results indicate that low-affinity enhancers actively transcribed far from the native svb locus also co-localize with microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from observation that relocated enhancers show Ubx enrichment similar to native locus

claim: Increasing the affinity of a single low-affinity binding site in the E3N enhancer decreased Ubx enrichment near transcription sites to 0.44 ± 0.27.
source: Consistent with these previous results, we observed that increasing the affinity of a single low-affinity binding site in the E3N enhancer decreased Ubx enrichment near transcription sites to 0.44 ± 0.27 (Figure 3I and J, E3N High Affinity, n = 36, three embryos).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis of mutant enhancer

claim: Deletion of two low-affinity sites in E3N results in active transcription in regions of increased Ubx enrichment (0.65 ± 0.18).
source: Consistent with this model, when we deleted two low-affinity sites in E3N, active transcription was observed in regions of increased Ubx enrichment (0.65 ± 0.18, Figure 3K and L, E3N Mut23, n = 62, five embryos).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis of mutant enhancer

claim: Deletion of two low-affinity Ubx sites from the 7hr enhancer did not alter Ubx enrichment around transcription sites (0.63 ± 0.37).
source: Deletion of two low-affinity Ubx sites from the 7 hr enhancer did not alter Ubx enrichment around transcription sites (0.63 ± 0.37, Figure 3O and P, 7H Mut23 n = 81, six embryos).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis of mutant enhancer

claim: Deletion of three Ubx-binding sites in the 7H enhancer increased relative Ubx enrichment to 0.91 ± 0.27.
source: But, deletion of three Ubx-binding sites in the 7H enhancer increased relative Ubx enrichment, consistent with the pattern we observed for the E3N enhancer (0.91 ± 0.27, Figure 3Q and R, 7H Mut123, n = 52, eight embryos).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis of mutant enhancer

claim: There is an inverse correlation between binding site affinity and the distribution of Ubx intensities at transcription sites.
source: Across all manipulations, we observed an inverse correlation between binding site affinity and the distribution of Ubx intensities at transcription sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Analysis of Ubx intensity distributions across multiple enhancer variants with different affinities

claim: The number of Ubx-binding sites and their affinities determine the response of svb enhancers to local Ubx concentration.
source: Thus, the number of Ubx-binding sites and their affinities determine the response of svb enhancers to local Ubx concentration.
evidence: Inferred from systematic manipulation of binding site number and affinity showing corresponding changes in Ubx enrichment

claim: Lower affinity enhancers require higher Ubx concentrations to drive transcription.
source: Lower affinity enhancers require higher Ubx concentrations to drive transcription.
evidence: Inferred from observation that enhancers with deleted binding sites show higher Ubx enrichment at transcription sites

claim: Higher affinity enhancers can drive transcription at lower local Ubx concentrations.
source: Conversely, higher affinity enhancers can drive transcription at lower local Ubx concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from observation that enhancers with increased binding site affinity show lower Ubx enrichment at transcription sites

claim: Enhancers may be dynamically sampling local nuclear environments.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that enhancers may be dynamically sampling local nuclear environments.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed relationship between enhancer affinity and Ubx concentration requirements

claim: A lower fraction of nuclei showing transcription from enhancers with binding site deletions may occur because there are fewer areas of the nucleus in which peak Ubx levels are sufficient for weakened svb elements.
source: A lower fraction of nuclei showing transcription from enhancers with binding site deletions (Figure 3K,O,Q) may occur because there are fewer areas of the nucleus in which peak Ubx levels are sufficient for weakened svb elements.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed reduction in transcription frequency with weakened enhancers

claim: Ubx requires Hth/Exd to bind to the low-affinity sites in 7H and E3N in vitro.
source: In vitro, Ubx requires Hth/Exd to bind to the low-affinity sites in 7H and E3N (Crocker et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to previously published in vitro binding studies

claim: Hth deficiency leads to loss of expression for both 7H and E3N enhancers in vivo.
source: In vivo, Hth deficiency led to the loss of expression for both 7H and E3N (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Expression analysis in Hth mutant embryos showing loss of enhancer activity

claim: Hth is co-enriched with Ubx around active transcription sites driven by 7H or E3N.
source: Consistent with this requirement for both Ubx and Hth, Hth was co-enriched with Ubx around active transcription sites driven by 7H or E3N (Figure 4E–T).
evidence: Co-immunofluorescence and FISH data showing spatial colocalization of Ubx and Hth at transcription sites

claim: The relative enrichment for Ubx and Hth at 7H transcription sites is 0.58 ± 0.14 and 0.41 ± 0.16, respectively.
source: The relative enrichment for Ubx and Hth, respectively, was 0.58 ± 0.14 and 0.41 ± 0.16 for 7H (n = 51, seven embryos) and 0.66 ± 0.13 and 0.39 ± 0.24 for E3N (n = 74, five embryos).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis

claim: The relative enrichment for Ubx and Hth at E3N transcription sites is 0.66 ± 0.13 and 0.39 ± 0.24, respectively.
source: The relative enrichment for Ubx and Hth, respectively, was 0.58 ± 0.14 and 0.41 ± 0.16 for 7H (n = 51, seven embryos) and 0.66 ± 0.13 and 0.39 ± 0.24 for E3N (n = 74, five embryos).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from radial distribution analysis

claim: Transcription from co-factor-dependent enhancers requires microenvironments that contain high concentrations of both transcription factors and their co-factors.
source: These results suggest that transcription from co-factor-dependent enhancers requires microenvironments that contain high concentrations of both transcription factors and their co-factors.
evidence: Inferred from observation that both Ubx and Hth are co-enriched at transcription sites of enhancers requiring both factors

claim: Transcription factor microenvironments are present as multiple highly differentiated transcription domains containing unique combinations of transcription factors.
source: This observation provides further support for the model that transcription factor microenvironments are present as multiple highly differentiated transcription domains containing unique combinations of transcription factors.
evidence: Inferred from the specific co-enrichment of Ubx and Hth at sites requiring both factors

claim: Microenvironments of high local concentrations of transcription factors and their co-factors may circumvent the instability of low-affinity interactions by promoting more frequent DNA binding and cooperative interactions.
source: Microenvironments (Reiter et al., 2017) of high local concentrations of transcription factors and their co-factors may circumvent the instability of low-affinity interactions by promoting more frequent DNA binding and cooperative interactions when enhancers are located within these domains (Farley et al., 2016) (Figure 4U and V).
evidence: Speculative mechanistic model based on observed colocalization patterns and known principles of molecular interactions

claim: Microenvironments may be relatively stable domains generated by rapid dynamics of individual molecules.
source: These microenvironments may be relatively stable domains generated by rapid dynamics of individual molecules.
evidence: Speculative interpretation reconciling observed stable colocalization with rapid single-molecule dynamics

claim: Unique microenvironments may have relatively long half-lives.
source: In contrast, the fact that svb enhancers placed on the third chromosome often co-localized with the native svb locus on the X chromosome suggests that unique microenvironments may have relatively long half-lives.
evidence: Inferred from observation that enhancers on different chromosomes colocalize

claim: Clustered binding sites for the same transcription factor could lengthen the dwell time of proteins near enhancers and increase effective local protein concentrations.
source: First, clustered binding sites for the same transcription factor (Crocker et al., 2016b) could lengthen the dwell time of proteins near enhancers and increase effective local protein concentrations (Yao et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2006; Elf et al., 2007; Kabata et al., 1993; Leith et al., 2012; Ruusala and Crothers, 1992).
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to relevant literature

claim: Cooperative and scaffolding interactions between transcription factors and co-factors can stabilize transcription factors at low-affinity sites.
source: Second, cooperative and scaffolding interactions between transcription factors and co-factors, each of which may bind independently to enhancers, can stabilize transcription factors at low-affinity sites (Farley et al., 2016; Junion et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to relevant literature

claim: Clustering of enhancers could trap transcription factors over longer length scales, perhaps generating the ~200 nm microenvironments observed.
source: Finally, clustering of enhancers could trap transcription factors over longer length scales (Noordermeer et al., 2014; de Laat and Duboule, 2013; Symmons et al., 2016; Williamson et al., 2016; Giorgetti et al., 2016), perhaps generating the ~200 nm microenvironments that we observed.
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to relevant literature and consistent with observed microenvironment size

claim: Multiple promoters can share the same enhancer in a common local environment.
source: This last model is supported by recent findings that multiple promoters can share the same enhancer in a common local environment (Fukaya et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to published study supporting the enhancer clustering model

claim: Transcription factor microenvironments may be a general feature of eukaryotic transcription.
source: Transcription factor microenvironments may be a general feature of eukaryotic transcription, as supported by studies showing mouse and human cells exhibiting RNA polymerase II crowding (Cisse et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2016), transcription factors using local clustering to efficiently find their binding sites (Liu et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014), and chromatin packaging in Drosophila cells generating distinct chromatin environments at the kilobase-to-megabase scale (Boettiger et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative generalization supported by citations to studies in multiple organisms

claim: Mouse and human cells exhibit RNA polymerase II crowding.
source: Transcription factor microenvironments may be a general feature of eukaryotic transcription, as supported by studies showing mouse and human cells exhibiting RNA polymerase II crowding (Cisse et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2016), transcription factors using local clustering to efficiently find their binding sites (Liu et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014), and chromatin packaging in Drosophila cells generating distinct chromatin environments at the kilobase-to-megabase scale (Boettiger et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to published studies in mammalian cells

claim: Transcription factors use local clustering to efficiently find their binding sites.
source: Transcription factor microenvironments may be a general feature of eukaryotic transcription, as supported by studies showing mouse and human cells exhibiting RNA polymerase II crowding (Cisse et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2016), transcription factors using local clustering to efficiently find their binding sites (Liu et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014), and chromatin packaging in Drosophila cells generating distinct chromatin environments at the kilobase-to-megabase scale (Boettiger et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to published studies on transcription factor dynamics

claim: Chromatin packaging in Drosophila cells generates distinct chromatin environments at the kilobase-to-megabase scale.
source: Transcription factor microenvironments may be a general feature of eukaryotic transcription, as supported by studies showing mouse and human cells exhibiting RNA polymerase II crowding (Cisse et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2016), transcription factors using local clustering to efficiently find their binding sites (Liu et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014), and chromatin packaging in Drosophila cells generating distinct chromatin environments at the kilobase-to-megabase scale (Boettiger et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to published study on chromatin organization

claim: These findings are consistent with a phase-separated model of transcriptional regulation whereby distinct microenvironments contain different combinations of proteins inside the nucleus.
source: Collectively, these findings are consistent with a phase-separated model of transcriptional regulation (Hnisz et al., 2017) whereby distinct microenvironments contain different combinations of proteins inside the nucleus.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in context of phase separation model from literature

claim: Localized regions impose a spatial constraint on the expression of genes, allowing transcriptional activation from enhancers only when they are physically in regions with the correct combinations of transcription factors and co-factors.
source: These localized regions impose a spatial constraint on the expression of genes, allowing transcriptional activation from enhancers only when they are physically in regions with the correct combinations of transcription factors and co-factors.
evidence: Speculative model based on observed spatial organization and factor requirements

claim: Multiple enhancers acting as DNA scaffolds for protein binding could provide the anchoring interactions that form transcriptional microenvironments.
source: Multiple enhancers acting as DNA scaffolds for protein binding could provide the anchoring interactions that form transcriptional microenvironments.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic model for microenvironment formation

claim: Microenvironments provide a mechanism to allow both efficient and specific transcription from low-affinity enhancers.
source: These microenvironments would, in turn, provide a mechanism to allow both efficient and specific transcription from low-affinity enhancers.
evidence: Speculative functional interpretation of microenvironment role

claim: Protein-DNA binding is often an ephemeral event with transcription factors dissociating within seconds of binding to DNA in mammalian cells.
source: Protein-DNA binding is often an ephemeral event; studies in mammalian cells demonstrate that transcription factors disassociate within seconds of binding to DNA (Liu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Izeddin et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2011; Normanno et al., 2015; Morisaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to multiple published studies on transcription factor binding dynamics

claim: Low-affinity DNA-binding sites are critical to confer specificity between related transcription factors having binding sites with similar DNA sequences.
source: Furthermore, recent studies in animals ranging from fruit flies to mammals have revealed that low-affinity DNA-binding sites are critical to confer specificity between related transcription factors having binding sites with similar DNA sequences (Crocker et al., 2015; Farley et al., 2015; Farley et al., 2016; Lorberbaum et al., 2016; Antosova et al., 2016; Rister et al., 2015; Crocker et al., 2010; Crocker et al., 2016b; Tanay, 2006; Lebrecht et al., 2005; Rowan et al., 2010; Gaudet and Mango, 2002; Jiang and Levine, 1993).
evidence: Citation to multiple published studies across different organisms

claim: Increasing the affinity of binding sites to more stably recruit transcription factors activates promiscuous gene expression.
source: Increasing the affinity of binding sites to more stably recruit transcription factors activates promiscuous gene expression (Farley et al., 2015; Ramos and Barolo, 2013), which leads to developmental defects.
evidence: Citation to published studies showing consequences of increased binding site affinity

claim: Promiscuous gene expression from high-affinity binding sites leads to developmental defects.
source: Increasing the affinity of binding sites to more stably recruit transcription factors activates promiscuous gene expression (Farley et al., 2015; Ramos and Barolo, 2013), which leads to developmental defects.
evidence: Citation to published studies showing phenotypic consequences

claim: The shavenbaby (svb) locus contains multiple enhancers that drive specific patterns of svb gene expression in developing Drosophila embryos.
source: We have explored this problem using the shavenbaby (svb) locus, which contains multiple enhancers that drive specific patterns of svb gene expression in developing Drosophila embryos.
evidence: Description of the experimental system used in the study

claim: Each of three characterized svb enhancers contains clusters of low-affinity binding sites for the Hox gene Ultrabithorax (Ubx).
source: Each of three characterized svb enhancers contains clusters of low-affinity binding sites for the Hox gene Ultrabithorax (Ubx).
evidence: Description of enhancer composition based on prior characterization

claim: svb enhancers require the Ubx cofactor Homothorax (Hth) to function.
source: These enhancers also require a Ubx cofactor Homothorax (Hth) to function (Crocker et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to previous study establishing Hth requirement

claim: Enhancers are genomic regions near coding genes that direct specific patterns of gene expression.
source: Genomic regions near coding genes, called enhancers, direct specific patterns of gene expression (Spitz and Furlong, 2012; Reiter et al., 2017; Long et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to published reviews on enhancer function

claim: Enhancers contain short DNA sequences that bind sequence-specific activating and repressive transcription factor proteins.
source: Enhancers contain short DNA sequences that bind sequence-specific activating and repressive transcription factor proteins, and the integration of these positive and negative signals directs gene expression (Crocker et al., 2016a).
evidence: Citation to published work on enhancer composition and function

claim: The integration of positive and negative signals from transcription factors directs gene expression.
source: Enhancers contain short DNA sequences that bind sequence-specific activating and repressive transcription factor proteins, and the integration of these positive and negative signals directs gene expression (Crocker et al., 2016a).
evidence: Citation to published work on enhancer function

claim: The homeodomain proteins Extradenticle (Exd)/Pbx and Homothorax (Hth)/MEIS interact with Ubx during DNA binding.
source: The homeodomain proteins Extradenticle (Exd)/Pbx and Homothorax (Hth)/MEIS (Slattery et al., 2011b; Rieckhof et al., 1997; Ryoo and Mann, 1999; Lelli et al., 2011) interact with Ubx during DNA binding, and Ubx and Hth regulate a partially overlapping set of genes (Choo et al., 2011; Slattery et al., 2011a).
evidence: Citation to multiple published studies on Hox cofactor interactions

claim: Ubx and Hth regulate a partially overlapping set of genes.
source: The homeodomain proteins Extradenticle (Exd)/Pbx and Homothorax (Hth)/MEIS (Slattery et al., 2011b; Rieckhof et al., 1997; Ryoo and Mann, 1999; Lelli et al., 2011) interact with Ubx during DNA binding, and Ubx and Hth regulate a partially overlapping set of genes (Choo et al., 2011; Slattery et al., 2011a).
evidence: Citation to published genomic studies

claim: Airyscan imaging provides 1.7-fold higher resolution compared to diffraction-limited confocal imaging.
source: Fixed Drosophila embryos mounted in ProLong Gold mounting media (Molecular Probes, Eugene, OR) were imaged on a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope with Airyscan (Carl Zeiss Microscopy, Jena, Germany) using 3D Airyscan in SR mode to obtain images with 1.7-fold higher resolution compared to diffraction-limited confocal imaging (Sheppard et al., 2013) (method supplements: imaging setup for Airyscan).
evidence: Citation to technical specification of imaging method

claim: JF635 is minimally fluorescent in solution but its fluorescence increases by over 100-fold when bound to a HaloTag protein.
source: JF635 is minimally fluorescent in solution but its fluorescence increases by over 100-fold when bound to a HaloTag protein, allowing the detection of labeled Ubx molecules against a background of dim freely diffusing dyes.
evidence: Description of dye properties based on characterization

claim: Embryos were expanded by approximately four-fold in each dimension using expansion microscopy.
source: To observe Ubx distribution at higher resolution, we expanded the size of the embryos (Tillberg et al., 2016) by approximately four-fold in each dimension (Figure 1C).
evidence: Description of expansion microscopy protocol with citation and measurement

claim: Ubx and Hth did not co-localize throughout the nucleus despite being co-enriched near enhancers that require Hth.
source: The Ubx cofactor, Homothorax (Hth), was co-enriched with Ubx near enhancers that require Hth, even though Ubx and Hth did not co-localize throughout the nucleus.
evidence: Implicit comparison between local enrichment at specific sites versus global nuclear distribution

claim: Mechanisms that generate transcription factor microenvironments could be a general feature of eukaryotic transcriptional regulation.
source: Mechanisms that generate these microenvironments could be a general feature of eukaryotic transcriptional regulation.
evidence: Speculative generalization based on findings in Drosophila and supporting evidence from other systems

claim: The transcription factor Ultrabithorax (Ubx) utilizes low-affinity binding sites in the Drosophila melanogaster shavenbaby (svb) locus and related enhancers in nuclear microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations.
source: Here, we report that the transcription factor Ultrabithorax (Ubx) utilizes low-affinity binding sites in the Drosophila melanogaster shavenbaby (svb) locus and related enhancers in nuclear microenvironments of high Ubx concentrations.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding supported by multiple experimental observations

claim: Related enhancers colocalize to the same microenvironments independently of their chromosomal location.
source: Related enhancers colocalize to the same microenvironments independently of their chromosomal location, suggesting that microenvironments are highly differentiated transcription domains.
evidence: Summary of double-FISH experimental findings

claim: There is an inverse relationship between enhancer affinity and Ubx concentration required for transcriptional activation.
source: Manipulating the affinity of svb enhancers revealed an inverse relationship between enhancer affinity and Ubx concentration required for transcriptional activation.
evidence: Summary of systematic enhancer manipulation experiments
